essay:
# A reading both sides predicted settles nothing.

Two forecasters can watch the same number climb and both be right, because each of them predicted it. Most arguments about where AI goes next are like that: the evidence each side points to fits the other side's story too. For each question the outlook turns on, this page sets out what named writers argue, what each side expects this site's readings to show, what they show tonight, and the reading that would tell the sides apart.

### Folio I · Can AI do whole jobs, reliably?

## Fast progress on single skills is what both sides expect; whole jobs are the test

The fastest story starts with a loop. Daniel Kokotajlo, who worked on governance at OpenAI, and his fellow forecasters at the AI Futures Project wrote AI 2027, a dated story in which each AI model, a program trained on text and data to write and reason, helps build the next, so progress feeds on itself until AI outdoes people at almost everything by the end of 2027 [cite:ai_2027]. They called 2027 their single most likely year rather than their middle estimate. They pushed their dates later at the end of 2025 and moved them earlier again in 2026, because coding agents, models set to carry out tasks on their own, had improved faster than they expected in late 2025 and early 2026 [cite:ai_futures_update]; their own check finds events running a little slower than the story [cite:ai_futures_q25].

Benjamin Jones, an economist at Northwestern who studies where growth and discoveries come from, answers with arithmetic. Research is a chain of steps and needs every one of them, so making some steps superhumanly fast leaves the rest, still slow, to set the pace, as a line of walkers moves at the speed of its slowest member. In his words, "bottlenecks severely mute the effect of extremely productive AI" [cite:jones_b]. What counts is the share of steps AI can take over.

Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor and their colleagues, Arvind Narayanan among them, computer scientists at Princeton who test AI agents, add that getting a task right is not getting it right every time: agents that solve more tasks each year still give different answers when the same task is run again, and agents must be dependable, not just accurate, before they are given work that matters [cite:agent_reliability]. Princeton's tracker of AI agents, which this site reads, scores each agent's accuracy and reliability from nought to one, and across the agents it has tested accuracy has risen by [fact:hal_accuracy_trend] and reliability by [fact:hal_reliability_trend], where a point is a hundredth of that range. AI 2027's story also has agents stumbling in their first years, so the gap settles nothing yet.

[plate:reliability]

The fastest clock settles nothing either. The length of the software tasks AI can finish doubles every [fact:horizon_doubling], at least as fast as AI 2027 assumed, but neither side doubts that single skills race ahead. Whole jobs separate them. On the Remote Labor Index, which scores models on real paid freelance projects completed end to end, the best model manages [fact:rli_record]. The compounding story, as written, needs most of those projects done by the end of 2027; the slowest-step story expects whole projects to trail single skills for years.

[plate:frontier]

### Folio II · Who checks the work?

## Whether checking AI's work becomes a business turns on who must answer for it

Markets run on knowing whom you are dealing with. Gillian Hadfield, who designs legal and regulatory systems for AI, and Andrew Koh, who studies how to design markets, point out that AI agents have none of the identity, registration or records that markets rely on, and sketch two routes, each with its own problems: tie each agent to a person or firm that answers for it, or give it legal standing and assets a court could seize [cite:hadfield_koh]. This site carries their argument one step further: if someone must answer for an agent's work, someone may be paid to check it. In February 2026 Gartner, which advises companies on what to buy, published a guide to the firms that sell platforms for testing and watching AI systems, and since January 2026 insurers have been able to attach optional standard wording that excludes harm from generative AI, the kind that writes and draws, from their general liability policies [cite:iso_exclusions]. The rival view is that the labs, the companies that build the most capable models, and the big cloud companies, which rent out computing, give checking away with their own platforms, and no reading yet tells the two apart.

Soren Larson, who writes about how money moves between the labs and the apps built on them and co-founded Crosshatch, a personalised-AI start-up that shut down in 2025, thinks apps that resell a lab's models by the token get squeezed. An app reselling a lab's model pays at least the lab's own price per token, the fragment of a word in which the use of a model is sold, and can charge little more than going to the lab directly would cost, so its margin, what is left of revenue after the cost of what was sold, shrinks towards whatever its own additions are worth [cite:larson_squeeze]. His argument rests on one observation: "To my knowledge labs do not offer special wholesale pricing" [cite:larson_squeeze]. Nobody publishes app margins, so it cannot be tested yet.

Platforms face the mirror image. Peyman Shahidi, John Horton and their colleagues, economists and a computer scientist who study online markets, one of whom, Andrey Fradkin, works for Amazon, argue that agents could slash the cost of searching and bargaining, and expect platforms to set rules for how outside agents may use them, much as websites tell search engines' crawlers, the programs that read the web for them, what they may read [cite:shahidi_etal]. Byrne Hobart and Nikhil Davar, who write The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology, in an issue that discloses a holding in Amazon, read Amazon's blocking of Meta's shopping assistant in September 2026 as a sign that platforms gain enough from controlling their customers' dealings with AI to keep outside agents out [cite:hobart_inference]. Amazon had already gone to court in November 2025 to keep Perplexity's shopping agent off its site, while Etsy and Walmart agreed to let shoppers buy through OpenAI's chatbot. This site's hand-kept ledger for the past year puts fences at [fact:fences_ledger] and openings at [fact:openings_ledger], but it does not yet sweep both sides under one rule, so it tests nothing yet.

### Folio III · Is adoption slow, or just hard to see?

## Adoption at the pace of past technologies fits both stories, so the argument turns on what the statistics miss

Narayanan and Kapoor's larger argument is that AI is a normal technology, whose big effects on the economy will come over decades, at the pace at which people and institutions change how they work [cite:normal_tech]. The Census Bureau's survey of American businesses fits their account so far: [fact:firms_using_ai] of firms say they used AI somewhere in their business in the past two weeks, in line with the pace of past technologies rather than faster. History suggests the harder part comes after arrival. Diego Comin and Martí Mestieri, economists who study how technologies spread between countries, found that the delay before new technologies reach poor countries has narrowed towards rich countries', but that poor countries use them far less intensively, and that this gap in depth explains most of the widening of the income gap since 1820 [cite:comin_mestieri].

[plate:adoption]

Diane Coyle and John Lourenze Poquiz, economists at Cambridge who study how the economy is measured, reply that most use of AI is free and its gains come as better work and saved time, which the official statistics do not price, so measured output can lag, or even fall, while people are better off [cite:coyle_poquiz]. Set against ChatGPT's weekly users, OpenAI's paying subscribers come to [fact:paid_share]; the two are different counts, so this is not the share of users who pay, but it shows that most weekly users pay nothing. That fits both stories: people may not pay because the tool is not yet worth much, or because its value never passes through a till.

The clearest early sign may be in hiring. Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen, economists at Stanford who study AI and work through payroll records, found that workers in their early twenties in the jobs most exposed to AI have fallen behind their less exposed peers, mostly because firms hire fewer of them [cite:canaries]. They describe the pattern without claiming to have proved its cause, so the comparison carries the weight. With each group's employment set at a hundred in November 2022, the young now stand at [fact:junior_gap] against workers over fifty in the most exposed fifth of jobs, and at [fact:junior_gap_control] in the least exposed. If the gap opened everywhere, something other than AI would be the likelier culprit.

### Folio IV · Does work reorganise fast enough to show up in output?

## Two economists have bet against an explosion, and tonight's reading is one both sides expected

The cleanest test here is a bet. Benjamin Moll, an economist at the London School of Economics who studies whole economies, and Alex Imas, a behavioural economist who leads the economics of advanced AI at Google DeepMind, on leave from Chicago Booth, are bullish on what AI will be able to do and still think growth of more than ten percent a year in the next decade or so extremely unlikely, since it would need several unlikely things at once, from fast automation across the economy to AI that automates research itself [cite:moll_imas]. In August 2026 they and five others took the other side of a bet from four people who bet, at odds of four to one against them, that in some quarter before 2034 American real output per person, output after inflation divided by the population, will stand [test:bet_fast_side] or more above the highest level it had reached a year or more before [cite:bet_fast_side]. Among the four is William MacAskill, a moral philosopher and senior research fellow at Forethought, a research group on advanced AI, who with Fin Moorhouse, then a researcher at Forethought and now at Google DeepMind, has argued that AI could compress a century of technological progress into a decade [cite:macaskill_moorhouse]. Tonight output per person stands [fact:gdp_pc_over_peak] above that level [cite:moll_imas_bet].

Charles Jones and Christopher Tonetti, economists at Stanford who study long-run growth, supply the slow side's arithmetic: work is a chain of tasks that substitute poorly for one another, so if AI follows the pattern of past automation, growth rises only slowly, to less than three percent a year even by 2075, while in their fastest calibration, in which machines everywhere improve as fast as they have in making computers, it passes seven percent by 2030, though even then output explodes only decades later [cite:jones_tonetti]. Nor would a fast path necessarily show early. Anton Korinek, Charles Jones and colleagues, economists who model growth under advanced AI, several of whom work for or advise Anthropic, turned assumptions about AI into paths for the economy, which they present as scenarios rather than forecasts, and found that "Across scenarios, almost all of the divergence comes after 2027" [cite:korinek_etal].

Even where AI works, the first thing it changes may not be hours. In 1930 John Maynard Keynes, whose work founded modern macroeconomics, suggested that within a century people might share out the little work left in a week of about fifteen hours [cite:keynes]. Betsey Stevenson, a labour economist at Michigan, expects the opposite order: the washing machine raised the standard of a clean house long before it shortened the hours spent on housework, and AI, she argues, will first raise how much people are expected to do [cite:stevenson].

The bet settles it by early 2034 at the latest. Output per person grew by [fact:gdp_pc_yoy] in the latest year, close to Jones and Tonetti's slow path [cite:jones_tonetti], though a reading like that fits the fastest of Korinek and colleagues' scenarios until about 2027 as well.

### Folio V · Who keeps the money?

## Whether the labs keep their margins turns on how fast open models catch up

Carlota Perez, an economist who studies technological revolutions and the financial bubbles that come with them, found the same sequence in each great surge of technology since 1771 that had run its course: a frenzy of investment that runs ahead of the uses, a crash, then a golden age in which the technology is put to work; writing in 2002, she placed the fifth, the information age, at the turning point after its crash [cite:perez]. The builders of the infrastructure rarely keep the value, note Arvind Narayanan and Akash Kapur, a senior fellow at New America who studies how AI is governed, with cloud computing and the leading chip foundry, a factory that makes chips for others, as partial exceptions. Selling access to the frontier models, the most capable ones, tends towards a commodity business, where buyers choose on price alone, so the labs' likeliest escape, they argue, is to move up the stack, into products and deployments built into their customers' work, where switching is costly [cite:nk_up_the_stack].

Hobart sets out when models become a commodity: once some labs give away open models, whose inner workings anyone may download and run, the marginal cost of serving the cheapest models comes down to the chips and power that run them, and a model has more pricing power where it is the best tool for a particular job [cite:hobart_round_trip] [cite:hobart_pacing]. Larson adds that even the best model need not be bid down, with a result from Simon Board and Marek Pycia, economists who study how sellers set prices over time. A monopolist selling something that lasts is usually forced to cut its price by buyers who wait for discounts; but if every buyer has another option, "the seller charges a constant price in every period equal to the monopoly price" [cite:board_pycia], the price it would charge if it could promise never to cut it, given what buyers can get elsewhere. For AI, the open model is the other option: the lab keeps charging for its lead and lets the buyers who will not pay go, though as open models close the gap its price and its market both shrink, and if they improve fast enough that buyers would rather wait for them, a pace he judges low, it is bid down after all [cite:larson_durability].

The readings so far fit both. Open models carry [fact:open_share] of the tokens routed to the busiest models on OpenRouter, a marketplace that passes developers' requests to many models, and trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag]. At list prices, among the open models that can be matched with a closed one as capable, the labs' own cheaper models even undercut them, costing a median [fact:open_premium] as much, though that is a single reading so far. Meanwhile NVIDIA and AMD take [fact:chips_gp_share] of the gross profit, revenue less the direct cost of what was sold, that they share with Microsoft's cloud arm and the estimates for OpenAI and Anthropic, the only cloud and lab figures this site can measure, and the biggest cloud and platform companies spend [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much a year on buildings and equipment as AI earns in revenue. David Cahn, an investor at Sequoia Capital, has raised, every year since 2023, his estimate of the revenue AI must eventually earn to pay back a year of that spending, though he now sees in AI's help with writing code a clearer way to earn it [cite:cahn_2026].

[plate:stack]

What the labs do with the best model's price while it still leads will settle it. If they cut it towards the open models' to keep its sales, Narayanan and Kapur's commodity view wins; if they keep a premium for the lead and let buyers go, Larson's does, though he expects even that premium to give way if open models improve fast enough that buyers wait for them.

### Where they agree

## A handful of points recur across these writers, and not only on one side

Selling access to a model that others can match, token by token, is a thin business; someone has to answer for what an AI agent does before it can be trusted with work that matters; checking AI's work becomes a costly task of its own; and people use AI well before firms reorganise around it. Where someone here dissents, the dissent is listed with the point.

### The futures still open

## Crossing progress with rules shows which futures tonight's readings still allow

How fast capability improves and how the rules on deploying AI settle will decide which future arrives. So far the rules have got lighter: the American president ordered moves against state AI laws in December 2025 [cite:eo_14365], Colorado replaced its AI Act with a narrower law on automated decisions in May 2026 [cite:colorado_sb26_189], and the European Union put off its rules for high-risk AI until the end of 2027 and beyond [cite:eu_2026_1744]. Kapoor and Narayanan had argued years earlier that licensing who may build models would not work [cite:nk_licensing].

The grid crosses the two and fills a cell only where a named writer argues it; a cell stays open while none of its signposts is failing its test, and every open cell is marked, never just one. What would close cells, and change the outlook: whole paid projects done end to end, labs cutting the best model's price or keeping a premium while it still leads, independent firms winning the checking, platforms fencing or opening, and output per person breaking away before 2030.

positions.kill_shot: Customers becoming bound to one lab by exclusive deals and bans on copying.

positions.mechanism: Labs compete for users and revenue, so a model kept back is revenue handed to a rival.

positions.mechanism: Each fall in price makes AI worth using for more work, and use grows faster than the price falls.

positions.mechanism: Work gets moved to cheaper models and fixed routines, so falling prices cut the bill faster than new uses add to it.

positions.kill_shot: NVIDIA's revenue staying almost wholly one-off sales of hardware.
positions.mechanism: NVIDIA lends to and invests in the data centres that buy its chips in return for a share of their income, turning one-off sales into a stream and gaining a say over who gets capacity.
positions.title: NVIDIA finances its customers

positions.case: Labs and clouds already buy capacity from one another in every direction.
positions.kill_shot: The largest firms keeping their computing for their own use and renting none of it out.
positions.mechanism: The largest technology firms build more computing than they need and rent the spare to rivals, turning each firm's bet into one bet, shared across the industry, that demand for AI keeps growing.
positions.title: The builders overbuild and rent out the rest

positions.case: Search shows how much advertisers pay for a clear sign of what someone wants; assistants can see that want earlier.
positions.kill_shot: Ads in assistants driving users away or earning far less per user than ads in search.
positions.mechanism: Assistants can see what people want to buy earlier than search does, so advertisers will pay to reach them, and ads fund the free versions.
positions.title: Advertising pays for free AI

positions.case: Firms build more of their own software with coding agents while still running on the same systems of record.
positions.kill_shot: Software that holds a business's records losing customers as fast as other software.
positions.mechanism: Coding agents let firms build their own tools instead of buying them, but the programs that hold a business's core records are hard to replace and every new tool needs them.
positions.title: The software that keeps the records gains

positions.case: The labs keep adding engineers who work inside customers' firms.
positions.kill_shot: Labs reporting gross margins as high as software firms' while running large teams inside their customers.
positions.mechanism: Labs need staff inside their customers to deploy their models, and that staff grows with the customers.
positions.title: Deployment staff pull the labs' margins down

positions.case: Firms buy AI for any task where it returns more than it costs, however small.
positions.kill_shot: New businesses in small information niches not rising as AI's costs fall.
positions.mechanism: Once a task costs less by machine than any worker would, services appear that were never worth paying a person for, and growth comes from filling them.
positions.title: Cheap AI fills niches no one served

positions.case: Firms building around AI hire for range more than for depth.
positions.kill_shot: Specialists keeping their value over versatile workers.
positions.mechanism: When AI does the specialised steps, the valuable worker is the one who can direct it across many of them.
positions.title: Versatile workers pull ahead of specialists

anchors.text: The American president ordered moves against state AI laws and called for a light national standard.
Standard exclusions for harm caused by generative AI became available for insurers to attach to general liability policies.
Colorado replaced its AI Act with a narrower law on automated decisions, which applies from January 2027.
The European Union's changes to its AI Act came into force, putting off its rules for high-risk AI until December 2027 and August 2028.

cells.says: Scaling runs out before whole jobs are in reach, and the gains come from spreading what already works.
The spending outruns the revenue it needs, and the losses fall on the investors who paid for it.
Capability keeps improving, firms adopt it at the pace of past technologies, and growth rises without exploding.
Clear rules settle who pays for AI's mistakes, and adoption speeds up where they do.
Agents and the firms behind them must register before they deal; licensing who may build the models, Kapoor and Narayanan argue, would not work.
Each model speeds up the research behind the next and output breaks away; in Restrepo's model, wages then settle at the cost of the computing that could replace a person.
In the story's slower ending, a committee of the leading lab and the government slows the race until the systems can be checked.
Either a race produces systems nobody can check, or people are slowly made irrelevant as AI takes over the work, thought and choices that gave them a say.

rules.label: Courts and insurers price the risk

sources.field: forecasters of AI progress at the AI Futures Project; Kokotajlo worked on governance at OpenAI
sources.finding: A dated story in which AI labs use each model to speed up the research that builds the next, ending with AI that outdoes people at almost everything by the end of 2027. The authors say 2027 was their single most likely year, and their middle estimates were later.
sources.who: Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland, Thomas Larsen and Romeo Dean, with Scott Alexander

sources.field: forecasters at the AI Futures Project, revising their own dates
sources.finding: After pushing their dates for fully automated coding later at the end of 2025, the forecasters brought them forward again, because AI coding agents improved faster than they expected in late 2025 and early 2026.
sources.who: Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland and Brendan Halstead
sources.work: Q1 2026 Timelines Update

sources.field: forecasters at the AI Futures Project, checking their story against events
sources.finding: Checked against what has happened, the story is roughly on track but running a little slower, at roughly seventy to ninety percent of its pace.
sources.who: Eli Lifland, Daniel Kokotajlo and Brendan Halstead
sources.work: Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update: Uplift and Revenue

sources.field: an economist at Northwestern who studies where growth and scientific progress come from
sources.finding: Research needs every step done, so an AI that is superhumanly good at some steps lifts overall progress only a little while other steps stay slow; what counts is the share of steps it can take over. He adds that checking the work becomes a task of its own, and that AI able to check its own work could reduce the need for costly human checking.
sources.quote: bottlenecks severely mute the effect of extremely productive AI
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: Artificial Intelligence in Research and Development

sources.field: Princeton researchers who test AI agents
sources.finding: Large gains in how often agents solve tasks brought only small gains in how dependably they do it; agents still answer differently on repeat runs and break when instructions are reworded, and though their stated confidence is better calibrated, they still often cannot tell when they will fail.
sources.who: Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor and colleagues, including Arvind Narayanan
sources.work: Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability

sources.field: Hadfield designs legal and regulatory systems for AI; Koh studies how to design markets and incentives
sources.finding: AI agents lack the identity and registration systems markets rely on; the authors sketch two routes, each with its own problems, one tying each agent to a registered person or firm that answers for it, the other giving agents legal standing with assets a court could seize.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: An Economy of AI Agents

sources.field: a writer for the Independent Insurance Agents and Brokers of America, reporting on the standard policy wordings that ISO, a unit of Verisk, drafts for insurers
sources.finding: New optional endorsements with a January 2026 edition date let insurers exclude harm arising from generative AI from general liability policies; each insurer chooses whether to attach them.
sources.work: Verisk to Roll Out New General Liability Exclusions for Generative AI Exposures

sources.field: a writer on how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them, who co-founded Crosshatch, a personalised-AI start-up that shut down in July 2025
sources.finding: Apps that resell a lab's models are squeezed between the lab's price per token and what customers would pay to go to the lab directly, so as use grows their profit shrinks towards nothing unless their revenue stops tracking tokens.
sources.quote: To my knowledge labs do not offer special wholesale pricing
sources.work: The Smart Squeeze

sources.field: economists and a computer scientist who study online markets; Fradkin works for Amazon and Horton advises Anthropic
sources.finding: Agents could slash the cost of searching, bargaining and contracting; they will be taken up first where people already hire human agents and can state simply what they want, and platforms will set rules for how outside agents may use them, much as websites tell search engines' crawlers what they may read, though some already block them.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.who: Peyman Shahidi, Gili Rusak, Benjamin Manning, Andrey Fradkin and John Horton
sources.work: The Coasean Singularity? Demand, Supply, and Market Design with AI Agents

sources.field: writers of The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology; the issue discloses a holding in Amazon
sources.finding: Amazon blocked Meta's shopping assistant from its site; the authors read it as a sign that companies gain enough from controlling their customers' dealings with AI to pay for the computing themselves rather than let another firm's agent in.
sources.work: Forward Deployed (the section Fighting for Inference)

sources.field: computer scientists at Princeton who study what AI can and cannot do
sources.finding: AI's large effects on the economy will arrive over decades, at the pace at which people and institutions adopt it, as with electricity and the internet. Unclear liability deters firms from adopting a technology, and clear rules can speed it up.
sources.work: AI as Normal Technology

sources.field: economists who study how technologies spread between countries
sources.finding: Across two centuries, the delay before new technologies reach poor countries has narrowed towards rich countries', but poor countries use them far less intensively, and that gap in the depth of use explains most of the widening of the income gap since 1820.
sources.work: If Technology Has Arrived Everywhere, Why Has Income Diverged?

sources.field: economists at Cambridge who study how the economy is measured
sources.finding: Official statistics will capture AI's contribution poorly and late, because most use is free and its gains in quality and saved time are not priced, so measured output can lag or even fall while people are better off.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.who: Diane Coyle and John Lourenze Poquiz
sources.work: Making AI Count: The Next Measurement Frontier

sources.field: economists at Stanford's Digital Economy Lab who study AI and work through payroll records
sources.finding: Employment of workers in their early twenties in the jobs most exposed to AI has fallen behind that of their less exposed peers, mostly through less hiring, while experienced workers show no such gap. The authors describe the pattern; they do not claim to have proved its cause.
sources.who: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen
sources.work: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence

sources.field: Moll is a macroeconomist at the London School of Economics; Imas, a behavioural economist, leads the economics of advanced AI at Google DeepMind, on leave from Chicago Booth
sources.finding: Growth of more than ten percent a year in the next decade or so is extremely unlikely even if AI's abilities leap, because it would need several unlikely things at once, from fast automation across the economy to AI that automates research itself; four to five percent a year would already be massive. They are bullish on AI's abilities and have bet against an explosion.
sources.work: Will AI soon lead to double-digit growth?

sources.field: the four who took the fast side of the growth bet; MacAskill is a moral philosopher at Forethought, a research group that studies how to prepare for advanced AI
sources.finding: They bet, at odds of four to one against them, that in some quarter before 2034 American real output per person will stand fifteen percent or more above the highest level it had reached a year or more before.
sources.short: the fast side of the growth bet
sources.who: William MacAskill, Samuel Albanie, Tom Cohen and Jan Kulveit
sources.work: Bet on Explosive AI-Driven Growth

sources.field: MacAskill, a moral philosopher who taught at Oxford until 2024, is a senior research fellow at Forethought, a research group that studies how to prepare for advanced AI; Moorhouse was a researcher there until June 2026 and is now at Google DeepMind
sources.finding: Once AI's thinking rivals the whole of humanity's, it will keep growing far faster than the number of people, so a century of technological progress could be compressed into a decade, followed by an explosion in industry.
sources.work: Preparing for the Intelligence Explosion

sources.field: the terms of a public bet agreed in August 2026
sources.finding: Seven people, Moll and Imas among them, bet against four others that in no quarter before 2034 will American real output per person stand fifteen percent or more above the highest level it had reached a year or more before; the fast side wins as soon as one quarter does, later revisions do not reopen a settled bet, a reading close to the line waits for the government's third estimate, and disputes go to an arbiter.
sources.who: Benjamin Moll, Alex Imas and five others
sources.work: Bet on Explosive AI-Driven Growth

sources.field: economists at Stanford who study long-run growth
sources.finding: Past automation raised productivity through ever better machines, but work is a chain of tasks that substitute poorly for one another, so weak links tame the explosion; if AI follows the pattern of past automation, growth rises only slowly, and even if machines everywhere improve as fast as they have in making computers, growth passes seven percent by 2030 but explodes only decades later.
sources.work: Past Automation and Future A.I.: How Weak Links Tame the Growth Explosion

sources.field: economists who model growth under advanced AI; several work for or advise Anthropic
sources.finding: A model that turns assumptions about AI into paths for the economy to 2030, from barely changed to growing far faster than today; the authors present them as scenarios, not predictions.
sources.quote: Across scenarios, almost all of the divergence comes after 2027.
sources.who: Anton Korinek, Charles Jones, Szymon Sacher, Tess Cotter and Peter McCrory
sources.work: Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI

sources.field: the economist whose work founded modern macroeconomics
sources.finding: Within a century, barring important wars and any large increase in population, technical progress might raise living standards so far that the economic problem would be solved, or at least be within sight of solution; and he suggested people might share out the little work left in three-hour shifts, a fifteen-hour week.
sources.venue: an essay, reprinted in his Essays in Persuasion
sources.work: Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren

sources.field: a labour economist at the University of Michigan
sources.finding: The danger is not too little output but gains that reach many people late and unevenly; as with household appliances, AI will first raise how hard and how well people work before it frees their time.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: What Is There to Fear in a Post-AGI World?

sources.field: an economist who studies technological revolutions and the financial bubbles that come with them
sources.finding: Each great surge of technology since 1771 that has run its course went the same way, a frenzy of investment that runs ahead of the technology's uses, a crash and a remaking of the rules, then a golden age in which the technology is put to work; writing in 2002, she placed the fifth, the information age, at the turning point after its crash.
sources.work: Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital

sources.field: Narayanan is a Princeton computer scientist; Kapur, a senior fellow at New America, studies how AI is governed
sources.finding: Selling access to frontier models tends towards a commodity business, where competition likely pushes prices to cost, so the labs' likeliest path to lasting profit is moving up the stack into products and deployments built into their customers' work, which escapes the trap at the price of lock-in. The builders of past infrastructure rarely kept the value, with cloud computing and the leading chip foundry as partial exceptions.
sources.work: Up the Stack: How AI's Escape From the Commodity Trap Risks Enterprise Lock-in

sources.field: the writer of The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology, after work in digital advertising and investment research
sources.finding: Once some AI labs give their models away as open weights, the marginal cost of serving the cheapest models comes down to the chips and power that run them; he reads a chip-equipment maker's investment in an open-model lab as keeping AI labs many and chip demand high.
sources.work: The Autistic Half-Century (the section Round-Tripping)

sources.field: the writer of The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology, after work in digital advertising and investment research; he discloses that he holds shares in Alphabet
sources.finding: Models have more pricing power where they are the best tool for a particular job; labs that agree to slow their best releases are also agreeing not to widen their lead over open models.
sources.work: The Economics and Politics of Pacing the Frontier

sources.field: economic theorists who study bargaining and how sellers set prices over time
sources.finding: A monopolist selling a durable good is normally forced down by buyers who wait for discounts; when every buyer can take another option instead, the only equilibrium is the seller charging the monopoly price every period, a price set against what buyers can get elsewhere.
sources.quote: the seller charges a constant price in every period equal to the monopoly price
sources.work: Outside Options and the Failure of the Coase Conjecture

sources.field: a writer on how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them, who co-founded Crosshatch, a personalised-AI start-up that shut down in July 2025
sources.finding: Applying Board and Pycia, buyers who will not pay a lab's price leave for an open model rather than wait for a discount, so the lab keeps charging a monopoly price instead of being bid down by waiting buyers; but that price reflects only its lead over the open alternative, so as open models close the gap its price and its market both shrink, and its revenue erodes faster than its lead; and if open models improve fast enough that buyers would rather wait for them, a pace he judges low, the lab is bid down after all, so he doubts today's high margins will last.
sources.work: Durability of Frontier AI

sources.field: an investor at Sequoia Capital who backs AI and infrastructure companies
sources.finding: His running estimate of the revenue needed to pay back each year's spending has grown every year since he first posed the question in 2023, though he now sees in AI's help with writing code a clearer way to earn it back.
sources.work: AI's $1.5T Question

sources.field: an executive order
sources.finding: Calls for a light national standard for AI, to be proposed to Congress, and moves against state AI laws through a federal task force to challenge them in court, a list of burdensome state laws and conditions on federal grants; it names Colorado's law as the kind it means.
sources.who: The President of the United States
sources.work: Executive Order 14365: Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence

sources.field: a state law
sources.finding: Repeals the state's AI Act and replaces it with a narrower law on automated decisions about jobs, housing, lending and the like, from January 2027.
sources.work: SB26-189, Automated Decision-Making Technology

sources.field: a regulation amending the EU's AI Act
sources.finding: Simplifies the AI Act and puts off its rules for high-risk AI, to December 2027 for the high-risk uses the Act lists and August 2028 for AI built into regulated products.
sources.who: The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union
sources.work: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI

sources.field: computer scientists at Princeton who study what AI can and cannot do
sources.finding: Licensing who may build powerful AI models would need ever more intrusive surveillance as training gets cheaper, and would leave only a handful of firms able to build the most capable models.
sources.work: Licensing is neither feasible nor effective for addressing AI risks

sources.field: a machine-learning researcher who builds and writes about open language models
sources.finding: AI already helps build AI, but the loop leaks, because the research it can automate is narrow, adding agents gives less and less, and the judgement of a few top researchers still sets the pace; so he expects progress, looked back on, to seem closer to a steady line than an explosion.
sources.work: Lossy self-improvement

sources.field: computer scientists at Princeton who study what AI can and cannot do
sources.finding: Scale has brought new abilities before, but scaling laws predict only how well a model guesses the next word, not which abilities appear, and good data is getting ever costlier, so making models bigger is unlikely on its own to produce general intelligence.
sources.work: AI scaling myths

sources.field: an investor and writer who works in the market for training data
sources.finding: The scarce input is realistic, well-checked training data, meaning practice tasks, grading rubrics and quality checks for long work whose results are hard to verify.
sources.work: An AI Bubble is a human data problem

sources.field: a writer on how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them, who co-founded Crosshatch, a personalised-AI start-up that shut down in July 2025
sources.finding: Cheap agents make dealing with outsiders costlier, not cheaper, because asking a market for anything reveals what you want to your competitors; so firms keep work inside, platforms shut out outside agents, and firms split into the very large and the very small.
sources.work: Against The Coasean Singularity

sources.field: a behavioural economist who leads the economics of advanced AI at Google DeepMind, on leave from Chicago Booth
sources.finding: As AI makes mass-produced things cheap and people richer, spending and jobs shift towards relational work, where the person doing it is part of the value, such as care, teaching and hospitality.
sources.work: What will be scarce?

sources.field: a Yale economist who studies how technology shapes work and pay, and a member of Anthropic's economic advisory council
sources.finding: Once AI can turn computing power into any kind of work, wages settle at what the computing to replace a person costs and labour's share of income heads towards nothing even as total wages rise; the path is jagged when better algorithms, not more computing, set the pace.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: We Won't Be Missed: Work and Growth in the AGI World

sources.field: economists who study competition and technology; both served as chief economist of the US antitrust division
sources.finding: When AI is sold by firms with market power, the workers it displaces can lose twice, once when cheap AI cuts their pay and again when its price later rises.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.who: Susan Athey and Fiona Scott Morton
sources.work: Artificial Intelligence, Competition, and Welfare

sources.field: Brynjolfsson directs Stanford's Digital Economy Lab; Hitzig studies AI's effects on society, now at the Anthropic Institute and at OpenAI when the chapter was written
sources.finding: AI can capture the local, unwritten knowledge that once argued for leaving decisions to people on the spot, so decisions centralise, with bigger firms, more concentrated industries and less room for local managers.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: AI's Use of Knowledge in Society

sources.field: an economist who studied how prices carry what people know
sources.finding: The knowledge an economy runs on is scattered among the people on the spot and never exists whole in any one place, so decisions about particular circumstances have to be left to them, with prices telling them what they need to know.
sources.work: The Use of Knowledge in Society

sources.field: Stiglitz won the Nobel prize for work on markets where one side knows more than the other; Ventura-Bolet is a doctoral student in economics at Columbia
sources.finding: News and other information is paid for by visits, and AI that answers directly diverts them, so without rules on accountability, content moderation and intellectual property, less true information may be made.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: The Impact of AI and Digital Platforms on the Information Ecosystem

sources.field: the writer of The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology; he discloses that he holds shares in Meta and Alphabet
sources.finding: For the biggest social network, the ideal is not owning the best model but having the best distribution for models that are good enough, then selling its users up to better ones, built in-house or not.
sources.work: Rumor Markets (the section AI and Complements)

sources.field: a writer on how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them, who co-founded Crosshatch, a personalised-AI start-up that shut down in July 2025
sources.finding: A neutral router that pools many firms' checked outcomes learns to solve their problems, new kinds above all, faster than any one firm alone, so paying for AI by the outcome belongs with it; in his simulation the model was held fixed, and what won was a harness trained on other firms' outcomes.
sources.work: Router Power

sources.field: a Yale economist who studies growth and productivity, and who won the Nobel prize for bringing climate change into long-run economics
sources.finding: Across American nonfarm business from 1948 to 2001, innovators kept only a tiny share of the value their innovations created, by his central estimate about two cents in the dollar; most of it went to consumers through lower prices.
sources.venue: National Bureau of Economic Research working paper
sources.work: Schumpeterian Profits in the American Economy: Theory and Measurement

sources.field: an investor at Sequoia Capital who backs AI and infrastructure companies
sources.finding: The revenue AI must earn to pay back a year's spending on data centres runs far ahead of what it earns; the chips lose value fast and computing rented by the hour has little pricing power, so if the revenue comes late the investors take the loss, while founders building on cheap computing gain.
sources.work: AI's $600B Question

sources.field: an investor at Sequoia Capital who backs AI and infrastructure companies
sources.finding: Expects the coming year to bring delays, with data centres finished late while use keeps rising; the cloud companies storing new chips instead of installing them would be the sign the delays had begun.
sources.work: AI in 2026: A Tale of Two AIs

sources.field: the head of global equity research at Goldman Sachs, and a former analyst of chip makers
sources.finding: AI is exceptionally expensive, and to justify its costs it must solve complex problems it was not designed to solve, and its costs may not fall as many expect; the report puts the coming spending at over a trillion dollars, and he expected it to continue despite his doubts.
sources.venue: Goldman Sachs Top of Mind, issue 129
sources.work: Interview, in Gen AI: too much spend, too little benefit?

sources.field: the founder of an investment firm that holds stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic
sources.finding: The old worry that selling access to AI models would become a commodity business no longer matters; customers could switch between models but mostly do not, margins are high, and only a handful of labs will matter because staying at the frontier costs too much capital. The open question is whether the returns on the spending arrive in time.
sources.venue: Invest Like the Best, a podcast, on YouTube
sources.work: Inside Dan Sundheim's Bets on Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX

sources.field: economists who study technology, firms and productivity
sources.finding: A general-purpose technology needs large investments in new processes, skills and ways of doing business that the national accounts measure poorly, so measured productivity looks weak in the technology's early years and strong later, when the investments pay off.
sources.who: Erik Brynjolfsson, Daniel Rock and Chad Syverson
sources.work: The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies

sources.field: a company that stands between many websites and their visitors, reporting on its own traffic
sources.finding: AI companies' crawlers, the programs that read websites for them, take far more pages than they send visitors back, including on news and publication sites, where Anthropic's crawler took thousands of pages for each visitor it sent.
sources.work: A deeper look at AI crawlers: breaking down traffic by purpose and industry

sources.field: a company that stands between many websites and their visitors, reporting on its own traffic
sources.finding: Its count of pages crawled for each visitor sent back may overstate the gap where an app, such as Anthropic's, does not say where its visitors came from, by an amount it cannot tell.
sources.work: The crawl before the fall… of referrals: understanding AI's impact on content providers

sources.field: a news report
sources.finding: Cloudflare bought Human Native, a British start-up that handles payments from AI developers to the creators whose work they train on, to build a system in which AI developers pay for the content they use.
sources.work: Cloudflare acquires AI data marketplace Human Native

sources.field: a podcaster who interviews AI researchers and a researcher working with him, who trained small models on each year's recipes and data
sources.finding: In small models trained on each year's recipes from 2019 to 2025, most of the gain in how much a model learns per unit of computing came from better training data rather than better designs; whether that holds for the largest models, and whether data made by machines can keep it going, they leave open.
sources.work: Pretraining progress is mostly coming from data

sources.field: the chief executive of Microsoft, which sells access to many labs' models on its cloud
sources.finding: Every company should build AI models fitted to its own business rather than lean on a few labs, because a firm is a system that learns.
sources.quote: there should be as many models in the world as firms in the world
sources.venue: Business Insider (Katherine Li), as syndicated by Yahoo Tech, reporting his interview with Yash Patil of Applied Compute
sources.work: Microsoft's Satya Nadella says every company should build its own AI model

sources.field: computer scientists at Princeton who study what AI can and cannot do in practice
sources.finding: AI has not replaced software engineers because deciding what to build and answering for what ships do not shrink, and cheaper software raises demand for it, so demand for engineers may even rise.
sources.venue: the AI as Normal Technology newsletter
sources.work: Why AI hasn't replaced software engineers

sources.field: the chief executive of OpenAI
sources.finding: The industry has been too ambitious about timelines, because the economy changes more slowly than the technology.
sources.quote: The economy just has so much inertia.
sources.venue: The Next Web, reporting his interview on David Senra's podcast
sources.work: Sam Altman says AI still has not had its iPhone moment

sources.field: an investor and writer who works in the market for training data
sources.finding: Open models have caught up enough that firms will run systems of small models they train further on their own work, provided that further training keeps getting cheaper.
sources.work: Mythos, Small Models, and how they'll impact the frontier data industry

sources.field: an investor at Pace Capital who writes about where computing happens
sources.finding: For much everyday work the cheapest and fastest place to run AI will be the device that already holds the data, so demand for inference in distant data centres will turn over slowly, then suddenly.
sources.venue: an essay he shared as a public document
sources.work: The End of Cloud Inference

sources.field: economists who study taxation and the economics of AI
sources.finding: As AI takes over paid work, taxes on wages lose their base and taxes on spending carry more of the load, until machines consume enough of the output that taxing people's spending falls short too.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI, NBER
sources.who: Anton Korinek and Lee M. Lockwood
sources.work: Public Finance in the Age of AI, a primer

sources.field: an investor and writer who works in the market for training data
sources.finding: Training data is bought from many specialist sellers, each strong in one field or kind of data, and computing capacity cannot be multiplied overnight the way new fibre equipment multiplied internet bandwidth.
sources.work: New Age Commodities

sources.field: an investor and writer who works in the market for training data
sources.finding: Each fall in the price of a model widens the set of builders who can afford agent systems, so total demand for AI rises, and cheap AI opens services that were never worth paying a person for.
sources.work: Victoria 3 and why data markets must be unbundled

sources.field: an investor and writer who works in the market for training data
sources.finding: Practice tasks staged by contractors stop teaching models long work that is hard to check, in fields such as biology, security and matters of taste, so labs turn to records of real work inside firms.
sources.work: State of Data (March 2026)

sources.field: an investor and writer who works in the market for training data
sources.finding: Models keep differing in efficiency and in the kinds of input they handle, so they do not become an interchangeable utility.
sources.work: State of Data (April 2026)

sources.field: an investor and writer who works in the market for training data
sources.finding: Labs buy more of their training data straight from leading app companies and specialists, and the cost of switching labs will not grow enough to lock customers in.
sources.work: State of Data (May 2026)

sources.field: an investor and writer who works in the market for training data
sources.finding: With many agents working on a task at once, most valuable office work will turn on the cost of computing and the systems around it rather than on what models can do; labs' attempts to tie customers down will not last.
sources.work: State of Data (June 2026)

sources.field: an investor and writer who works in the market for training data
sources.finding: Leading hosts, data sellers and custom-training firms are converging on one business, tuning open models for firms; Chinese labs will not take the frontier lead while the tests and paying buyers are American.
